questions.title: Associate Company & Joint Venture Test
questions.sectionReference: Companies Act, 2013, Section 2(6) and its Explanation
questions.questionText: Alpha Ltd. holds 22% of the voting power in another company in a fiduciary capacity. It also holds a 35% interest in a joint venture agreement and participates in the decision-making process of the joint venture. Examine whether the company qualifies as an associate company under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.studentText:
Law Test - 1

1) As per Section 2(6) of the Companies Act, 2013
-> An associate company, in relation to another company, means a company in which the other company has significant influence but not a subsidiary company but includes joint venture company.

Here,
- Alpha Ltd holds 22% voting power in a fiduciary capacity.
- But this 22% must be excluded while determining significant influence.
- It also holds 35% interest and participates in decisions under a joint venture agreement.

Conclusion,
- It qualifies as an Associate Company as the definition explicitly includes joint venture.
questions.modelAnswer: Section 2(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines an associate company, in relation to another company, as a company in which that other company has significant influence but which is not its subsidiary; the term also includes a joint venture company. Significant influence means control of at least 20% of total voting power, or participation in business decisions under an agreement. The 22% voting power stated to be held in a fiduciary capacity should not be relied upon as Alpha Ltd.'s own significant influence. However, Alpha Ltd. has a 35% interest in a joint venture and participates in its decision-making process. The joint venture is expressly included within the definition of associate company. Therefore, on the facts given, the joint venture qualifies as an associate company of Alpha Ltd., provided it is not a subsidiary of Alpha Ltd.
questions.expectedConclusion: Yes. The joint venture qualifies as an associate company because it is a joint venture in which Alpha Ltd. has a 35% interest and participates in decision-making; the fiduciary holding does not need to be counted.

questions.title: Small Company Definition & Subsidiary Exclusion
questions.sectionReference: Companies Act, 2013, Section 2(85), read with Companies (Specification of Definitions Details) Rules, 2014, as amended
questions.questionText: Zest Services Private Limited is a subsidiary company. Its paid-up share capital is ₹8 crore and its turnover, as per the profit and loss account for the immediately preceding financial year, is ₹90 crore. Examine whether Zest Services Private Limited qualifies as a small company under the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.studentText:
2) As per Sec 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013
-> a "small company" means a company other than public company
- paid-up share capital does not exceed ten crore rupees
- turnover as per profit & loss account for the immediately preceding financial year does not exceed one hundred crore rupees.

Here,
- Zest Services Pvt. Ltd is a private company, its paid-up capital is 8 crore rupees which is within the limit.
- Also its turnover is 100 crore rupees which is also within the prescribed limit.
- But the definition of small company is not applicable to subsidiary company.

Conclusion,
- Zest Services Pvt Ltd qualifies as a small company but being a subsidiary it lose its status as small company.
questions.modelAnswer: Section 2(85) of the Companies Act, 2013 defines a small company as a company other than a public company that satisfies the prescribed paid-up share capital and turnover limits. However, the proviso expressly excludes a holding company and a subsidiary company, among other categories, from the definition. Zest Services Private Limited is stated to be a subsidiary company and is therefore excluded from the definition of a small company, irrespective of its financial figures. For context, from 1 December 2025 the prescribed limits were increased to paid-up share capital not exceeding ₹10 crore and turnover not exceeding ₹100 crore. Zest's figures fall within those current limits, but the subsidiary-company exclusion still prevents it from qualifying. If the question is intended for an examination attempt before 1 December 2025, the then-applicable lower limits also need to be considered; the subsidiary exclusion remains decisive in either case.
questions.expectedConclusion: No. Zest Services Private Limited is a subsidiary company, which is expressly excluded from the definition of a small company under Section 2(85).

questions.title: One Person Company Dual Membership Restriction
questions.questionText: Aman is already a member of one One Person Company (OPC). On the death of another OPC member on 1 October 2023, Aman becomes a member of that OPC as well. Examine whether Aman can continue as a member of both OPCs and state the time limit, if any, within which he must comply with the applicable provisions of the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.studentText:
3) As per the provisions of Companies Act, 2013
-> a natural person shall not be a member of more than one OPC at any point in time and shall not be a nominee of more than one OPC.
-> A member in an OPC becomes a member in another such company, such person shall meet the criteria within a period of 180 days.

Here,
- Aman was already a member of one OPC.
- By the death of Vikas on 1st October 2023, Aman became a member of the second OPC.
- This creates a situation of dual membership which is prohibited.

Conclusion,
- Aman must rectify the dual membership status within 180 days from 1st October 2023.
questions.modelAnswer: Rule 3(2) of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014 provides that a natural person shall not be a member of more than one One Person Company at any point of time and shall not be a nominee of more than one such company. Rule 3(3) provides an exception where a person who is a member of one OPC becomes a member of another OPC by virtue of being a nominee in that company. In such a case, the person must meet the eligibility requirement within 180 days. Accordingly, Aman cannot continue as a member of both OPCs beyond the permitted period. He must choose one OPC and cease to be a member of the other within 180 days from becoming a member of the second OPC. If the membership arose on 1 October 2023, the 180-day period would ordinarily run to 29 March 2024, subject to the applicable rules of date computation.
questions.expectedConclusion: Aman cannot continue as a member of both OPCs indefinitely. He must regularise his membership within 180 days of becoming a member of the second OPC.

questions.title: Reservation of Name of LLP & 3-Month Window
questions.sectionReference: Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, Sections 15 and 16; Limited Liability Partnership Rules, 2009, Rule 18 and current MCA RUN-LLP instructions
questions.questionText: Explain the provisions relating to the reservation of the name of a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) under Section 16 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, with reference to: (i) the circumstances in which an application for reservation of a name may be made; (ii) the form and fee requirements; (iii) the period for which the name may be reserved; and (iv) restrictions relating to undesirable or identical names.
questions.studentText:
4) As per Section 16 of the Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Act, 2008
-> A person may apply to the Registrar for reservation of a name in the following circumstances:
- As the name of a proposed LLP, or
- As the name to which an existing LLP proposes to change its name.

-> The application must be made in the prescribed form and manner along with prescribed fee.

-> Upon receiving such an application, the Registrar may reserve the name for a period of three months from the date of intimation by the Registrar.

-> No LLP shall be registered by a name which is
- undesirable, or
- identical or too nearly resembling to that of any other LLP or a company or registered trademark.
questions.modelAnswer: Under Section 16 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, a person may apply to the Registrar for reservation of (a) the name of a proposed LLP, or (b) a new name to which an existing LLP proposes to change its name. The application is made electronically through the prescribed MCA process, commonly the RUN-LLP (Reserve Unique Name–LLP) service, with the prescribed fee; the current normal fee shown in MCA instructions is ₹200 per application. Under Section 16(2), if the Registrar is satisfied that the proposed name is not liable to be rejected under Section 15(2), the Registrar may reserve it for three months from the date of intimation. A name may be refused if it is undesirable or identical with, or too nearly resembles, the name of another LLP or company, or conflicts with a registered trade mark or other applicable naming restrictions. The proposed name must therefore satisfy the statutory and prescribed naming conditions.
questions.expectedConclusion: A proposed or changed LLP name can be reserved through the prescribed MCA process for three months, subject to payment of the prescribed fee and compliance with the statutory restrictions on names.
keywordsMatched: change of name of existing LLP

questions.title: LLP Whistleblowing Protection & Penalty Waiver
questions.questionText: Mr. Aman, a partner of an LLP, has provided useful information during an investigation. A penalty of ₹1,25,000 has been imposed on him. He is also an employee of the LLP. Answer with reference to Section 31 of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008: (i) Can the Tribunal waive or reduce the penalty imposed on Mr. Aman? (ii) Can the LLP discharge, terminate or otherwise penalise him in his capacity as an employee for providing such information?
questions.studentText:
5) As per Section 31 of the Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Act, 2008
-> The Court or Tribunal may reduce or waive any penalty leviable against any partner or employee of a LLP, if
- such partner or employee of an LLP has provided useful information during investigation
- when any information given by any partner or employee leads to LLP or any partner or employee of such LLP being convicted.

i) Yes, the Tribunal has power to waive or reduce the penalty of ₹1,25,000 being imposed on Mr. Aman as he has provided useful information.

ii) No partner or employee of any LLP may be discharged, demoted or suspended against the terms and conditions of his LLP or employment.
Hence Mr. Aman cannot be suspended from the job by the LLP.
questions.modelAnswer: (i) Yes. Under Section 31(1) of the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008, the Court or Tribunal may reduce or waive any penalty leviable against a partner or employee of an LLP if it is satisfied that the person provided useful information during an investigation of the LLP, or that information given by the person leads to a conviction of the LLP or a partner/employee under the LLP Act or any other Act. Since Aman provided useful information during an investigation, the Tribunal may exercise this discretion to reduce or waive the penalty. Waiver or reduction is discretionary, not automatic. (ii) No. Section 31(2) protects a partner or employee from being discharged, demoted, suspended, threatened, harassed or otherwise discriminated against in the terms and conditions of the LLP relationship or employment merely because the person provided, or caused to be provided, information under Section 31(1). Therefore, the LLP cannot terminate or penalise Aman in his capacity as an employee merely for providing that information.
questions.expectedConclusion: The Tribunal may waive or reduce the ₹1,25,000 penalty, but it is discretionary. The LLP must not discharge or discriminate against Aman in his employment merely because he provided information under Section 31.

questions.title: Private Placement Allotment Timeline & 12% Interest
questions.questionText: A company received application money from its members on 20 March 2023 for the issue of securities through private placement. However, the company failed to allot the securities by 30 June 2023. Examine the validity of the members' objection regarding non-allotment of securities and determine whether they are entitled to claim interest on the application money. Support your answer with reference to Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.studentText:
6) As per Section 42 of the Companies Act, 2013
-> a company making an offer or invitation under private placement
- shall allot its securities within 60 days from the date of receipt of application
- if the company is unable to allot the securities within that period, it shall repay the application money with 15 days from the expiry of 60 days.
- if the company fails to repay, it is liable to repay that money with interest at the rate of 12% per annum from the expiry of 60th day.

Here,
- The application money from the members was received on 20th March 2023 and company did not make an allotment of share till 30th June 2023.

---

- Hence the company is liable to repay the amount along with 12% interest.

Conclusion,
- The objection raised by the members to non allotment of shares is valid but their claim to pay 15% interest is not valid.
questions.modelAnswer: Section 42(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 requires a company making a private placement to allot the securities within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money. If it is unable to allot within that period, it must repay the application money within 15 days from expiry of the 60-day period. If the company fails to repay within that additional 15-day period, it is liable to repay the money with interest at 12% per annum from expiry of the sixtieth day. Here, the money was received on 20 March 2023 and securities had not been allotted by 30 June 2023, well beyond the 60-day allotment period. The members' objection is therefore valid. If the application money was not refunded within the further 15-day period, the subscribers are entitled to repayment with interest at 12% per annum from expiry of the 60th day. Assuming the date of receipt is excluded in counting, the 60-day period ended on 19 May 2023 and the further 15-day refund period ended on 3 June 2023.
questions.expectedConclusion: The objection is valid. If the company did not refund within the additional 15 days after the 60-day period, the subscribers are entitled to 12% p.a. interest from expiry of the 60th day.

questions.title: Bonus Shares Issue from CRR & Free Reserves
questions.sectionReference: Companies Act, 2013, Section 63(1)–(3); Section 52(2)(a) for permitted use of securities premium
questions.questionText: A company has the following balances: Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR) ₹1,50,000; Securities Premium ₹90,000; Surplus in Statement of Profit and Loss ₹1,20,000; total ₹3,60,000. The company proposes to issue bonus shares in the ratio of 1:3. The face value of each share is ₹10 and there are 90,000 existing shares. (a) Identify the sources from which the company may issue bonus shares under Section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013. (b) Calculate the number and amount of bonus shares to be issued. (c) Can the company issue bonus shares before making the final call on partly paid-up shares? Explain.
questions.studentText:
7) As per Section 63 of the Companies Act, 2013
-> a company may issue fully paid-up bonus shares to its members out of
- Free Reserves
- Securities Premium
- Capital Redemption Reserve (CRR)
-> Bonus shares cannot be issued out of reserves created by revaluation of assets.
-> Bonus shares can be issued only when partly paid-up shares are made fully paid-up.

A) Particulars | ₹
CRR | 1,50,000
Securities Premium | 90,000
Surplus in Statement of Profit & Loss | 1,20,000
Total | 3,60,000

---

B. Bonus Ratio -> 1:3
Bonus Shares = 90,000 * 1/3 = 30,000 shares
Face value -> ₹10
Amount = 30,000 * 10 = ₹3,00,000

C. No, the company cannot issue Bonus Shares until final call was made.
The partly paid-up shares shall be converted into fully paid-up to issue Bonus Shares.
questions.modelAnswer: (a) Under Section 63(1), fully paid-up bonus shares may be issued out of: (i) free reserves; (ii) the securities premium account; or (iii) the capital redemption reserve account. Reserves created by revaluation of assets cannot be capitalised for issuing bonus shares. (b) A 1:3 bonus ratio means one bonus share for every three existing shares. Number of bonus shares = 90,000 ÷ 3 = 30,000 shares. Amount of bonus issue = 30,000 × ₹10 face value = ₹3,00,000. The stated balances total ₹3,60,000, which is sufficient, assuming the P&L surplus is available as a free reserve and the other statutory conditions are met. For illustration, the company could capitalise ₹1,50,000 from CRR, ₹90,000 from securities premium and ₹60,000 from eligible P&L surplus. (c) No. Under Section 63(2)(e), the company cannot capitalise profits or reserves for issuing fully paid-up bonus shares unless any partly paid-up shares outstanding on the date of allotment are made fully paid-up. Therefore, the final call must be made and the partly paid-up shares must be fully paid before the bonus shares are allotted.
questions.expectedConclusion: Permitted sources are free reserves, securities premium and CRR (not revaluation reserves). The company would issue 30,000 bonus shares of ₹10 each, amounting to ₹3,00,000. Any outstanding partly paid-up shares must be made fully paid before allotment.
keywordsMatched: partly paid-up shares made fully paid-up

questions.title: Share Application Money Deemed Deposit Under Rules
questions.sectionReference: Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, Rule 2(1)(c)(vii), Explanation; Companies Act, 2013, Section 42(6) where the offer is by private placement
questions.questionText: A company received ₹3,00,000 as application money towards the subscription of securities. The company failed to allot the securities within 60 days from the date of receipt of the application money and also failed to refund the amount within the prescribed additional 15 days. Examine whether the amount received will be treated as a deposit under the Companies Act, 2013.
questions.studentText:
8) As per the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013
-> Any amount received towards subscription to any securities including share application money is not a deposit.
-> If the securities for which application money was received cannot be allotted within 60 days from the date of receipt of application money and such application money is not refunded within 15 days, such amount shall be treated as a deposit.

Here,
- The company failed to allot security within 60 days and also failed to refund the money within 15 days grace period.

Conclusion,
- The amount of ₹3,00,000 will be treated as a deposit.
questions.modelAnswer: Under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii) of the Companies (Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 2014, application money or an advance received towards subscription of securities is excluded from the definition of deposit while the statutory conditions are met. The Explanation provides that such amount is deemed to be a deposit if securities are not allotted within 60 days of receipt of the application money or advance and the amount is not refunded to subscribers within 15 days from expiry of those 60 days. In this case, the company neither allotted the securities within 60 days nor refunded ₹3,00,000 within the further 15-day period. Therefore, the amount is treated as a deposit under the said Rule. If the transaction is a private placement governed by Section 42, the company may also be liable to repay the amount with interest at 12% per annum from expiry of the 60th day under Section 42(6).
questions.expectedConclusion: Yes. Since the securities were not allotted within 60 days and the application money was not refunded within the additional 15 days, ₹3,00,000 is deemed to be a deposit under Rule 2(1)(c)(vii).
